explanations.answer: Praise the name of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The writer says, "Give praise, O servants of the LORD; praise the name of the LORD." He says it right after "Hallelujah!" so he's clearly warmed up. I think a psalm that starts this loud is hard to ignore.

I get the pull, friend. After a long day of work, a rest sounds like a great plan. But the writer calls the servants of the LORD to something else. He says, "Give praise, O servants of the LORD; praise the name of the LORD." Praise is the whole assignment here.

explanations.answer: Go up to the house of God
explanations.explanation: Close, friend, since praise is in the neighborhood. But this verse doesn't send the servants anywhere. The writer says, "Give praise, O servants of the LORD; praise the name of the LORD." Nobody has to pack a bag for it.

I see where that comes from, friend. Feast days feel like prime praise time. But the verse never mentions feast days. It says, "Blessed be the name of the LORD both now and forevermore." Now and forevermore leaves no day off the calendar.

That's right, baker. The writer says, "Blessed be the name of the LORD both now and forevermore." Feast days never come up in the verse. Both now and forevermore covers a LOT more days than a feast calendar does.
You got it, baker. The writer says, "The LORD is exalted over all the nations, His glory above the heavens." Over all the nations AND above the heavens. That's a big reach, friend.

I can see why you'd pick it, friend. The temple is a place people connect with praising God. But this verse points somewhere else. It says, "…His glory above the heavens." The temple doesn't come up at all.

Good guess, friend, since Zion shows up in the psalms, like "Mount Zion, in the far north, the city of the great King." (Psalm 48:2) This one doesn't mention it, though. The writer says the LORD is "…exalted over all the nations, His glory above the heavens." Above the heavens is a whole lot higher than any one mountain.

That's the one, baker. The writer asks, "Who is like the LORD our God, the One enthroned on high?" I think he's asking it to make you say it out loud: nobody. He doesn't hand over a list of names. He lets the question hang there.

That's a fair thought, friend. The verse before did mention all the nations. But verse 4 says the LORD is "…exalted over all the nations…" So the kings of those nations aren't the answer to "Who is like the LORD our God…" I think the writer is expecting a different answer: no one.

I get it, friend. Angels sound like the closest thing to compare. But the writer doesn't name a single one. He asks, "Who is like the LORD our God, the One enthroned on high?" and leaves it open. I think the answer he expects is no one.

You got it, baker. The psalm says, "He humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth." Think about that. The One enthroned on high stoops to look at the heavens AND the earth. That's the God of this psalm.

I can see why this one tripped you. The LORD is enthroned on high with His glory above the heavens, so humbling sounds like a stretch. But the psalm says it plainly: "He humbles Himself to behold the heavens and the earth." So the statement is true.
That's it, baker. The psalm says, "He raises the poor from the dust…" The One enthroned on high reaches down for the poor. I think that's one of the best lines in the whole psalm.

I see why you'd go there, friend. Raising people up sounds like it could go to anybody. But the psalm says, "He raises the poor from the dust…" It doesn't say a word about the proud here, so the blank is poor.
Good thinking that the LORD is over the mighty, friend. But that's not what this line says. The verse says, "He raises the poor from the dust…" The poor are the ones He lifts here.

explanations.answer: With the princes of His people
explanations.explanation: You nailed it, baker. The psalm says He lifts the needy "…to seat them with nobles, with the princes of His people." They go from the dump to a seat with princes. That's a promotion no résumé could get you.

explanations.answer: At the gate of the city
explanations.explanation: Good try, friend. The city gate is a place where elders sat, like when Boaz goes up to the gate and sits down there. (Ruth 4:1) But this psalm doesn't mention a gate. It says He seats them "…with nobles, with the princes of His people."

explanations.answer: Among the servants of the king
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a decent step up, friend. But the psalm aims higher than that. It says He seats them "…with nobles, with the princes of His people." Servants of the king aren't mentioned at all. The psalm puts them with princes.

That's right, baker. The psalm says, "He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children." It doesn't tell us how it happens. It just gives us the picture of a joyful mother at home. Then comes the final "Hallelujah!"
I see the guess, friend. But the psalm isn't talking about money here. It says, "He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children." Her story is about a home and children.

Fair guess, friend, since the psalm has been looking at a wide world. But this verse doesn't call her foreign. It says, "He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children." The word you want is barren.
